## Direct answer

The government can place limits on freedom of speech under specific conditions outlined in the Constitution and laws [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3].

Hate speech, defamatory speech, and speech that undermines fundamental rights may be restricted under the law [Source 1] [Source 4].

## Why this is the legal position

- Article 19(2) of the Constitution of India lists the grounds on which the government can restrict free speech [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3].
- The Supreme Court has held that such speech lies outside the protective perimeter of Article 19(1)(a) and can be restrained [Source 1] [Source 4].

## How this applies to you

- These restrictions can be imposed only if they are by or under the authority of law, are reasonable, and are related to the purposes mentioned in Article 19(2) [Source 2] [Source 3].
- Speech that does not conform to the content of the right under Article 19(1)(a) may be restrained by the government [Source 1] [Source 4].

## What you can do now

1. To determine if a restriction is valid, check if it falls under one of the grounds listed in Article 19(2) and whether it meets the three-pronged test established by the Supreme Court [Source 2] [Source 3].
2. If you believe your speech has been unjustly restricted, you may seek legal recourse by challenging the restriction in court [Source 1] [Source 4].

## Direct answer

Yes, the Constitution of India guarantees equal treatment by the State [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3].

## Why this is the legal position

- Article 14 of the Constitution of India states that the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3].
- The Supreme Court has interpreted Article 14 to mean that the law must not make arbitrary distinctions between groups of people [Source 4].
- Article 39A of the Constitution of India also supports the principle of equal justice and free legal aid for all citizens [Source 5].

## What you can do now

1. If you believe a law is being applied unfairly, you can challenge it in court or seek legal advice [Source 6].

## Important limits

- Article 14 does not require identical treatment for all people, only that the law does not make improper or invidious distinctions [Source 4] [Source 6].
- The interpretation of Article 14 may vary depending on the specific circumstances of each case [Source 4] [Source 6].

## Direct answer

No, the State cannot take away your life or liberty without following the law [Source 1] [Source 2].

The right to life and personal liberty is considered a fundamental right and is protected by the Constitution [Source 3] [Source 1] [Source 2].

## Why this is the legal position

- Article 21 of the Constitution of India guarantees the right to life and personal liberty and states that no person shall be deprived of these except according to law [Source 3] [Source 1] [Source 2].
- The Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed that the right to life and liberty is a basic assumption of the rule of law and cannot be violated without legal authority [Source 4] [Source 1] [Source 2].

## How this applies to you

- This means that the State must follow a legal procedure established by law before taking away your life or liberty [Source 3] [Source 1] [Source 2].
- This means that any action by the State that affects your life or liberty must be backed by a law that is valid and in force [Source 4] [Source 1] [Source 2].

## What you can do now

1. If you believe your life or liberty is being taken away without legal procedure, you can file a writ petition in the Supreme Court or High Court [Source 1] [Source 2].
2. You can seek legal assistance from a lawyer or a human rights organization if you believe your rights under Article 21 are being violated [Source 1] [Source 2].

## Important limits

- The exact legal procedure may vary depending on the situation and the law in force at the time [Source 3] [Source 1] [Source 2].
- The interpretation of what constitutes a legal procedure may depend on the specific law and the circumstances of the case [Source 3] [Source 1] [Source 2].

## Direct answer

A person detained without trial has the right to be informed of the grounds for their arrest and to consult a legal practitioner of their choice [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3].

A person detained without trial must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours of arrest [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3].

## Why this is the legal position

- Article 22(1) of the Constitution of India provides that no person arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed of the grounds for their arrest [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3].
- Article 22(2) of the Constitution of India mandates that every person arrested and detained must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours of arrest [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3].

## How this applies to you

- This applies to all persons arrested and detained, except for enemy aliens and those under preventive detention [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3].

## Important limits

- Article 22(3) excludes enemy aliens and persons arrested under preventive detention laws from these protections [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3].
- This requirement does not apply to persons arrested under preventive detention laws or enemy aliens [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3].

1. If you witness untouchability, you can report it to the police or a human rights organization [Source 3] [Source 4].

## Direct answer

Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, sexual harassment includes physical contact and advances involving unwelcome and explicit sexual overtures [Source 1].

Sexual harassment also includes a demand or request for sexual favours under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [Source 1].

Showing pornography against the will of a woman is considered sexual harassment under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [Source 1].

Making sexually coloured remarks is considered sexual harassment under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [Source 1].

Under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, sexual harassment includes uttering any word or making any sound with the intention that it is heard by the child [Source 2].

Sexual harassment of a child includes making the child exhibit his body or any part of his body so as it is seen by the person or any other person, under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 [Source 2].

Showing any object to a child in any form or media for pornographic purposes is considered sexual harassment under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 [Source 2].

Repeatedly or constantly following or watching or contacting a child either directly or through electronic, digital or any other means is considered sexual harassment under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 [Source 2].

Threatening to use, in any form of media, a real or fabricated depiction of any part of the body of the child or the involvement of the child in a sexual act is considered sexual harassment under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 [Source 2].

Enticing a child for pornographic purposes or giving gratification therefor is considered sexual harassment under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 [Source 2].

The punishment for dowry death is imprisonment for a minimum of seven years, which may extend to life imprisonment [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3].

## Why this is the legal position

- Section 80(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 prescribes a minimum of seven years' imprisonment and a maximum of life imprisonment for dowry death [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3].

## How this applies to you

- This applies to a woman who dies within seven years of marriage due to burns, injury, or under abnormal circumstances, and it is shown that she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or his relatives for a dowry demand [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3].
- This punishment applies to anyone who commits dowry death, including the husband or his relatives who caused the death through cruelty or harassment for a dowry demand [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3].

## Important limits

- The punishment applies only if the death is proven to be dowry death, and the evidence must show that the death was caused by cruelty or harassment for a dowry demand [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3].
